slides.texte_overlay:
How to handle a rude boss
with class
Don't answer in the heat of the moment. "Let me look into that and come back to you." A calm delay protects you from saying something you'd regret, and it makes you look composed.
Ask for specifics. "Which part exactly needs to change?" Vague attacks are hard to fix. Specific feedback is easy. Asking for details turns a rude moment into a clear to-do list.
Keep a short written record. Date, what was said, what you agreed. Not to start a war, just to have facts. Calm people with facts always end up in a stronger position.
Talk to them privately, not in front of the team. "Can we chat for five minutes? I want to make sure we work well together." Most bosses soften fast when the audience is gone.
Keep your mind sharp outside work. I do five minutes a day of history, art or science. It reminds me there's a bigger world than one bad boss, and that keeps me calm.
slides.texte_sophia: I do five minutes a day on a micro-learning app like the Sophia app. History, art, science. It reminds me there's a bigger world than one bad boss, and that keeps me calm.

slides.texte_overlay: Do excellent work anyway. Rude bosses can argue with your tone, not with your results. Being the guy whose work is undeniable gives you options, inside the company or outside it.
Know when to leave. If nothing changes after a few calm conversations, start looking. Staying classy doesn't mean staying forever. Leave on good terms, with your head high.
